dish: Kurama-yama shōjin zen — temple vegetarian dishes served in red lacquered bowls
address: Kurama, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (halfway up the steps to Kurama-dera's main gate)
w: Shōjin-ryōri in an old farmhouse with an irori hearth, on the steps up to Kurama-dera. Inside Kyoto calls it the nicest place to eat in Kurama.

dish: Summer kawadoko kaiseki: salt-grilled ayu and amago tempura
w: Inn and restaurant founded in 1932 beside Kifune Shrine. It is one of Kibune's best-known kawadoko spots, serving meals on platforms over the river in summer and a momiji kaiseki out of season.

dish: Kyō-kaiseki of river fish kept live in Kibune spring water; hamo and yuba on the kawadoko
w: Inn and restaurant open since 1962. From May to September it serves kaiseki on river platforms, using river fish that are rested for 2–3 days in mountain spring water before cooking. The casual offshoot Sagenta reopened in 2024.

dish: Kaiseki and sukiyaki served on platforms over the Kibune river in summer
w: A friendly, scenic Kibune riverside restaurant that serves meals on platforms over the Kibune-gawa in the hot months.

dish: Tofu kaiseki of Saga tofu, overlooking the Ōi river
address: Arashiyama, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (upstream of Togetsukyō Bridge)
w: Seasonal tofu kaiseki in the former holiday villa of Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe, with views over the Ōi river gorge.

dish: Kikisake tasting set: 18 Fushimi sake poured at a 23 m counter
n: Fushimi Sakagura Kōji (伏見酒蔵小路)
w: An alley of eateries in the sake district with sake from 18 Fushimi breweries (about 120 labels) and food stalls to go with it, from oden to okonomiyaki.

dish: Three-sake flights of Fushimi jizake, chosen daily
n: Ginjō Shubō Abura-chō (吟醸酒房 油長)
address: Ōtesuji shōtengai, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (4 min walk from Fushimi-Momoyama Station)
w: A sake shop on the Ōtesuji arcade (opened 1923) stocking around 100 labels, most of Fushimi's local brews among them. The kikizake counter at the back pours tasting flights with snacks.

dish: Ultra-thick kotteri broth that clings to the noodles — the chain's original bowl
n: Tenkaippin Sōhonten (天下一品 総本店)
address: Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (Ichijōji ramen district; ~15 min walk from Ichijōji Station)
w: The original shop of the nationwide kotteri chain, often credited with starting Ichijōji's ramen boom. Fans hold that the broth is still best here.

dish: Mitarashi dango: five small rice dumplings on a skewer in a sweet soy glaze
n: Kamo Mitarashi Chaya (加茂みたらし茶屋), Shimogamo
address: Shimogamo, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (by the gate of Shimogamo Shrine)
w: A teahouse founded in 1922 outside Shimogamo Shrine, widely called the birthplace of mitarashi dango. The dumplings imitate the bubbles rising in the shrine's Mitarashi pond, and the shop is said to have created the sweet-soy glaze.

dish: Handmade Kyoto udon
address: Okazaki, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (near Heian Jingū and the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art)
w: An udon shop with queues every day since it opened in 2006, in the former home of the chef's grandmother near Heian Jingū. It has been recognised by international food guides.

dish: Omurice under a beefy demi-glace; hamburg steak and ebi-fry lunch sets
w: A yōshoku (Western-style) grill in the Heian Jingū/Okazaki area since 1961, best known for its demi-glace omurice.

dish: Teoke bentō: four seasonal Kyō-yasai dishes packed in a wooden hand-pail
w: A Kyoto ryōri house founded in 1899, known for its teoke bentō served in a wooden hand-pail, and for celebration meals such as okuizome and shichi-go-san.

dish: Blend coffee, mixed sandwiches and curry-rice sets at lacquer-craftsman tables
n: Shinshindō Kyōdai Kitamonmae (進々堂 京大北門前)
w: A Paris-style café opened in 1930 at Kyoto University's north gate, nicknamed the university's "second library". Its heavy tables are by lacquer artist Tatsuaki Kuroda.

dish: Inari-zushi with hemp seeds and sesame; the 'nene-una' set of inari, futomaki, saba-zushi, soba and eel; grilled sparrow and quail
address: Fukakusa, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (by the torii at the back approach to Fushimi Inari Taisha)
w: A Fushimi Inari eatery open since 1540; the name is said to have come from Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Its inari-zushi is the shrine's own dish, and it also sells grilled sparrow and quail skewers to go.

dish: Arashiyama's two sakura-mochi: one wrapped in a salted cherry leaf, one of sticky rice around koshi-an
n: Honke Sakura-mochi Kotokiki Chaya (琴きき茶屋), Arashiyama
address: Saga-Tenryūji, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (north end of Togetsukyō Bridge)
w: A sweet shop more than 100 years old at the north end of Togetsukyō, whose two kinds of sakura-mochi are an Arashiyama speciality.

dish: Oyakodon with a fluffy half-set egg in sweet dashi; nishin soba with herring simmered a full day
address: Shimogawara-dōri, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (about 10 min walk from Gion-Shijō Station)
w: A long-running noodle-and-donburi shop on Shimogawara-dōri near Kōdai-ji, where locals queue at lunch for the oyakodon.

dish: Curry udon
address: Gion, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (short walk from Gion-Shijō Station)
w: A low-key Gion udon shop popular with geiko and maiko. It is known for its curry udon and stays open until 2–3 a.m., so it is a usual stop after a night out.

dish: Awa-mochi: millet mochi pounded to order, one piece with koshi-an and one with kinako; eat it the same day
address: In front of Kitano Tenmangū, Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto
w: A wagashi shop facing Kitano Tenmangū with roughly 340 years of history. Its additive-free millet mochi is made only when ordered and keeps for one day. It is on Tabelog's 2023 Hyakumeiten sweets list.

dish: Nama-yuba don and the 'Toyouke-don' of tofu simmered sweet-savoury
n: Toyouke Chaya (とようけ茶屋), Kitano
address: In front of Kitano Tenmangū, Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto
w: The tofu restaurant of Toyoukeya Yamamoto, a tofu maker founded in 1897 opposite Kitano Tenmangū, which opened the restaurant in 1992 to serve its tofu fresh. Lunch only.

dish: Warabi-mochi kneaded by hand every morning; warabi-mochi parfait
address: Shinbashi-dōri, Gion, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (beside the Shirakawa canal)
w: A sweets parlour in a former Gion teahouse on the Shirakawa canal. It makes its warabi-mochi by hand each morning and uses Tokachi Dainagon azuki and Yoshino kuzu.

dish: Saba sugata-zushi: whole Sea of Japan mackerel pressed on rice
w: A Kyō-zushi shop opposite Yasaka Shrine, founded in the late Meiji era by a former craftsman of Izuu who was given leave to open his own shop. Its saba-zushi uses true mackerel from the Sea of Japan.

dish: About 80 original breads from a Coupe du Monde de la Boulangerie prize-winner
w: A bakery that draws bread fans from across Japan; owner-baker Jun Tamaki has taken top prizes at the Coupe du Monde de la Boulangerie. Closed Monday to Wednesday.

dish: Uji matcha cuisine: kaiseki courses cooked with matcha
n: Kyō-Uji Matcha Ryōri Tatsumiya (辰巳屋), Uji
w: Founded around 1840 as a tea merchant, this Uji house became a restaurant in 1912 and has cooked with Uji matcha for over a century.

dish: Tango barazushi: the region's layered sweet-mackerel festival sushi
w: A Japanese restaurant open for more than 80 years and known for barazushi, the local dish of the Tango region.

dish: Saga tofu — soft, silky, handmade with groundwater
n: Saga Tofu Morika (嵯峨豆腐 森嘉)
w: A tofu maker dating from the Ansei era (1850s) whose soft, smooth Saga tofu shaped Kyoto's idea of tofu. It appears in Kawabata Yasunari's novel Koto, and Arashiyama yudofu restaurants use its tofu.

dish: Natsukantō: summer-orange jelly set in the hollowed fruit (seasonal); tea-ceremony sweets
w: Arashiyama branch of a Kyoto tea-ceremony confectioner, with a tearoom serving seasonal sweets and, in summer, natural-ice kakigōri.

dish: Sake and otsumami at a classic Kyoto taishū-sakaba
w: A popular sakaba (drinking hall) opened in 1934 near Nishijin. Serai calls it the shrine of Kyoto's taishū-sakaba.

dish: Kyō-ryōri kaiseki at a ryōtei founded in 1764
w: A Fushimi ryōtei founded in 1764. In the 1868 Battle of Toba-Fushimi the Shinsengumi and Satsuma troops fought in the street outside, and bullet holes are still in the lattice of the entrance.

dish: Inari senbei: fox-mask crackers of white miso and sesame, baked one by one
n: Sōhonke Hōgyokudō (総本家 宝玉堂), Fushimi Inari
address: 27 Fukakusa Ichinotsubo-chō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (near Fushimi Inari Station)
w: The shop that originated inari senbei, the fox-face crackers sold around Fushimi Inari. Each is still baked by hand in a mould. Opens at 7:30.

dish: Kyō-kaiseki of Kibune river fish, served on the kawadoko in summer
w: A riverside ryokan-restaurant described as the birthplace of Kibune's kawadoko, the summer platforms built over the Kibune river. It serves full Kyoto courses built on river fish.

dish: River-fish courses (ayu, carp, eel) on the kawadoko, May–September
w: A Kibune riverside restaurant serving seasonal cooking on the river platforms from May 1 to September 30.

dish: Kawadoko dining over the Kibune river
w: One of Kibune's more elegant riverside inn-restaurants, with platforms over the clear Kibune river and a shuttle from Kibuneguchi Station.

dish: Ine buri (yellowtail): buri-don, buri-shabu, local-fish set meals
address: Ine Town Tourism Association 2F, Ine-chō, Kyoto Prefecture
w: A canteen above Ine's tourist office, looking out over the boathouses, serving fish from Ine Bay. Ine is one of Japan's three great yellowtail grounds.

dish: Sashimi and kaisen-don of the day's Ine Bay catch
n: Restaurant Funaya (レストラン舟屋), Ine
address: Michi-no-Eki Funaya-no-Sato Ine, Ine-chō, Kyoto Prefecture
w: A Japanese restaurant inside the Funaya-no-Sato roadside station, on a rise with a view over the whole of Ine Bay.

dish: Fresh Ine Bay fish chosen each morning by a former ryokan head chef
n: Oshokujidokoro Aburaya (お食事処 油屋), Ine
address: Michi-no-Eki Funaya-no-Sato Ine, Ine-chō, Kyoto Prefecture
w: An eatery run by the former head chef of an old Ine ryokan, who buys the fish each morning; the dining room looks down on the boathouses.

dish: Ayu (sweetfish) in summer, matsutake in autumn, botan-nabe (boar hot-pot) in winter
n: Ayu-jaya Hiranoya (鮎茶屋 平野屋), Saga-Toriimoto
address: Saga-Toriimoto, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (at the first torii of Atago Shrine)
w: A thatched teahouse at the first torii of the Atago pilgrim road. It has been a tea stop and ayu wholesaler since the Edo period and serves the seasons in turn: sweetfish in summer, matsutake in autumn, boar hot-pot in winter.

dish: Yudofu set only: Morika tofu in kombu broth
address: Saga-Tenryūji, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (in a Tenryū-ji sub-temple)
w: Yudofu served in a Tenryū-ji sub-temple, using smooth tofu from the Saga maker Morika. The menu is a single set.

dish: Shichikusa yudofu: tofu hot-pot with seven seasonal vegetables, as eaten by the monks
n: Ryōan-ji Seigen-in (龍安寺 西源院)
w: A sub-temple restaurant inside UNESCO-listed Ryōan-ji, where every seat looks onto the garden. It is known for its seven-vegetable yudofu.

dish: Salt-grilled ayu on a kawadoko over the Kiyotaki river
n: Takao Momijiya (高雄 もみぢ家)
address: Takao, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (at the foot of Mt Takao)
w: An inn-restaurant founded in 1907 at the entrance to Takao. Its annexe Kawa-no-an is reached by a private suspension bridge, and its river platforms jut out over the Kiyotaki.

dish: Chūka soba in a light chicken-and-vegetable broth simmered for hours
address: 49 Ichijōji Nishisuginomiya-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (5 min walk from Ichijōji Station)
w: One of the oldest shops on the Ichijōji ramen strip, open since 1971 and late into the night. It is known for its slow-simmered chicken broth.

dish: Pour-over coffee; the reservation-only 'Future of Coffee' course at Blue Bottle Studio
n: Blue Bottle Coffee Kyoto Cafe, Nanzen-ji
w: Blue Bottle's first Kansai café, opened in 2018 in a renovated machiya more than 100 years old near Nanzen-ji. Its reservation-only floor is the only one in Japan.

dish: Monthly namagashi with matcha in the standing tea-room; zenzai and the shop-only 'konohana mochi'
n: Kanō Shōjuan Kyoto Chashitsu-tō (叶 匠壽庵 京都茶室棟)
address: 2-1 Nyakuōji-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (on the Philosopher's Path canal)
w: The tea-room of the Ōmi confectioner Kanō Shōjuan, on the Philosopher's Path canal, with a garden view that changes through the seasons. The Kyoto Shimbun reported its reopening after five years closed.

dish: Daitoku-ji shōjin ryōri (fu, yuba, goma-dōfu); Daitoku-ji natto
w: A Daitoku-ji shōjin-ryōri house that has kept the temple's vegetarian cuisine for more than 500 years; its name is said to come from the Zen priest Ikkyū. It also sells Daitoku-ji natto, the fermented-bean speciality.

dish: Soba lunch after a Daitoku-ji visit
n: Murasakino Wakuden, Daitoku-ji (紫野和久傳 大徳寺店)
w: The Daitoku-ji shop of the Kyoto ryōtei house Wakuden. Wa-raku recommends it for soba after visiting the temple.

dish: House-roasted coffee, baked goods and a weekly lunch beneath majolica tiles
w: A café in an 80-year-old bathhouse, the former Fujinomori Onsen, which closed in 1998. It keeps the karahafu roof, coffered ceiling, majolica-tiled walls and the partition between the baths.

dish: Light Kyoto-style tempura of seasonal Kyoto ingredients
n: Tempura Yasaka Endō (天ぷら 八坂圓堂)
w: A tempura house in a sukiya building that carries on a 130-year-old family business begun as an ochaya, frying seasonal Kyoto produce very light.

dish: Shichimi tōgarashi blended to a family recipe; sansho
w: Kyoto's oldest shichimi specialist, founded in the Meireki era (1655–58) on the Kiyomizu-dera approach. Its spice blend began as the hot karashi-yu served to pilgrims training under Otowa Falls.

dish: Unajū of eel grilled over binchōtan with a secret tare
n: Unagi Hirokawa (うなぎ 廣川), Arashiyama
address: 44-1 Saga-Tenryūji Kitatsukurimichi-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (3 min walk from Randen Arashiyama Station)
w: An eel specialist on Arashiyama's main street, grilling over binchōtan charcoal. Expect queues or book ahead.

dish: Kakinoha-zushi: mackerel or salmon sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves
n: Kakinoha-sushi Honpo Tanaka, Nara Honten (柿の葉すし本舗たなか なら本店)
w: An old-established maker of kakinoha-zushi, Nara's persimmon-leaf sushi, sold from a single piece. It has an in-store tea room, Kakinoha Chaya.

dish: Kuzu-mochi and kuzu-kiri made to order from Yoshino hon-kuzu; kuzu udon
n: Yoshino Honkuzu Tenkyokudō Nara Honten (吉野本葛 天極堂 奈良本店)
address: Nara city (on the site of Tōdai-ji's former West Gate), Nara Prefecture
w: A 150-year-old refiner of Yoshino kuzu starch, which still uses the traditional Yoshino-zarashi bleaching method. Its Nara shop makes kuzu sweets and kuzu dishes to order.

dish: Nara chagayu ('okaisan') — rice porridge cooked in tea
n: Tō no Chaya (塔の茶屋), Naramachi
w: Open since around 1963, first beside Kōfuku-ji's five-storey pagoda and now in Naramachi, serving Nara's tea-gruel tradition of about 1,200 years.

dish: Hand-cut soba; purveyor to Enryaku-ji
n: Honke Tsuruki Soba (本家鶴㐂そば), Sakamoto
w: A soba shop in Enryaku-ji's gate town that has made hand-cut soba for about 290 years. Its 136-year-old building is a Registered Tangible Cultural Property.

dish: Wagashi and matcha in an Ōmi satoyama; seasonal lunch; wagashi-making
n: Kanō Shōjuan Sunainosato (叶 匠壽庵 寿長生の郷), Ōtsu
w: The Ōmi confectioner's satoyama estate, where the head office moved 40 years ago. It has orchards, a restaurant, a bakery-café and hands-on wagashi making.

dish: Tamba seasonal cooking: bamboo shoots, ayu and hamo, matsutake, wild boar
n: Tamba Shikisai Ryōri Miyamotoya (丹波四季菜料理 宮本屋), Kameoka
w: A restaurant at Yunohana Onsen open for more than 90 years. It cooks Kameoka's seasons in turn: bamboo shoots in spring, ayu and hamo in summer, matsutake in autumn, boar in winter.

dish: Ōhara shibazuke: eggplant pickled with red shiso, naturally lactic-fermented
n: Doi Shibazuke Honpo, Ōhara Honten (土井志ば漬本舗 大原本店)
w: The white-walled head shop of Ōhara's best-known shibazuke maker, where pickles are still fermented and aged naturally in the old way.

dish: Ao-shiba and aka-shiba pickles from Ōhara-grown shiso, without preservatives or colouring
w: A pickle shop on the Sanzen-in approach that still makes everything by hand, with no preservatives or colouring. Its green and red shiba pickles use Ōhara's own shiso.

dish: Mountain-vegetable tempura and nimono; the three-tier 'Michikusa' bentō
w: A gasshō-style inn-restaurant beside Sanzen-in cooking Ōhara's seasonal mountain vegetables. Its teahouse serves yomogi warabi-mochi.

dish: Ushiwaka-mochi: horse-chestnut mochi filled with koshi-an
address: 235 Kurama Honmachi, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (in front of Kurama Station)
w: A sweets shop about 100 years old at the gate of Kurama-dera. It is known for Ushiwaka-mochi, made with tochi nuts leached in lye.

dish: Unabe (eel and ginger soup with grilled leek) and uzōsui (eel porridge with mochi, burdock and shiitake)
address: Shichijō, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto (3 min walk from Keihan Shichijō Station, by Sanjūsangen-dō)
w: An eel house on the spot where Toyotomi Hideyoshi is said to have rested and taken off his straw sandals (waraji) on visits to Hōkō-ji. Its unabe and uzōsui courses are dishes Wa-raku counts among Kyoto's 'national-treasure' dishes.

dish: Ohagi in three kinds (kinako, koshi-an, tsubu-an), sold until gone
w: An ohagi shop founded in 1897 using Tokachi azuki and Shiga mochi rice, which often sells out within an hour of opening.

dish: Inari udon with sweet fried tofu, after the shrine's foxes; handmade warabi-mochi
w: A noodle shop on the Fushimi Inari approach, founded in the early Shōwa era and little changed since, known for its fox-themed inari udon.

dish: Kombu-dashi chazuke set at lunch; about 20 kombu-based small plates with Fushimi sake at night
address: 4-52 Minami-shinchi, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (by Keihan Chūshojima Station)
w: The café and bar of a kombu dealer founded in 1912: dashi cooking at lunch, and in the evening kombu small plates paired with local Fushimi sake.

dish: Tōji-mochi: soft mochi wrapped round red-bean paste; yomogi daifuku
w: A sweet shop at Tō-ji's gate since 1912. Its namesake mochi is the classic snack after visiting the temple; it opens at 7 a.m.

dish: Gyātei gozen: obanzai in many small bowls
n: Arashiyama Gyātei (嵐山 ぎゃあてい)
address: By Randen Arashiyama Station, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto
w: A lunch restaurant by Randen Arashiyama Station serving Kyoto obanzai home cooking, made by trained cooks, in a spread of colourful small dishes.

dish: Yudofu kaiseki with Morika tofu; homemade goma-dōfu
n: Kyō-ryōri Yudōfu Chikusen (京料理 ゆどうふ 竹仙), Seiryō-ji
address: In the grounds of Seiryō-ji (Saga Shakadō), Ukyō-ku, Kyoto
w: Yudofu kaiseki inside the precincts of Seiryō-ji, using smooth tofu from Morika nearby. Its homemade sesame tofu is also well regarded.

dish: Yudofu and Japanese tofu dishes
n: Yudōfu Takemura (湯どうふ 竹むら), Arashiyama
w: One of the cluster of yudofu restaurants around Saga-Arashiyama, open from lunch into the evening.
